# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden and Halden

This is the strongest document in the set. It directly tests the three open questions from earlier rounds: whether the gain lasts, whether the meetings mechanism holds up, and whether recorded hours undercount work. It also corrects the meta-analysis on a point of fact. Its conclusions are mostly well calibrated. The main weaknesses are that the "confirmed" mediation result comes from the same seven offices that generated the hypothesis, that the control arm was partly contaminated, and that it is unclear what the system logs actually measure.

## What it does well

- **It meets the standard Varga & Holm set.** Output from records, hours from logs, a randomised comparison, and a two-year horizon.
- **It reports a decline instead of claiming persistence.** The gain fell from 12.5% to 8.5–9.8%, and the authors say so.
- **The mediation test was registered before the 24-month outcomes existed,** with mediators and outcome specified in advance.
- **It reports a failure plainly.** The counter arm was ended, and the reasons and cost estimate are given.
- **It frames the Halden survivors as an upper bound** rather than presenting them as a general estimate.
- **It checks the meta-analysis's supplementary data.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the meta-analysis's duration claim could not support its conclusion.
- **It resolves my earlier baseline concern.** Meeting time at baseline was similar in treated and control offices (7.4 v 7.2 hours). The month-six gap was therefore caused by the trial, not a pre-existing imbalance.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Calculation | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| 24m per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| 24m per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Decline on timesheets | 9.8 / 12.5 | −22% ("about a quarter", roughly ✓) |

Two figures need explanation:

**1. Control meeting time.** Two of the seven control offices cut meeting time from 7.1 to 5.0 hours. That alone should pull the control average down by about 0.6 hours. The reported control change is only 7.2 → 7.0, which implies the other five control offices increased meeting time by about 0.4 hours each. That could be true, but it should be stated.

**2. The counter-arm cost estimate.** Treated counter staff worked 17% fewer hours with a 6.7% per-hour gain. Restoring output would need about 1 / (0.83 × 1.067) ≈ 1.13, or roughly 13% more staff. The stated 12% is close. But 12% more staff at full pay would raise labour cost per contact by about 12%, not 9%. The 9% only works if labour is about three-quarters of total cost per contact. That is plausible, but it should be said.

## Issues

### 1. The mediation test confirms the hypothesis on the same offices that generated it

The hypothesis came from month-six data in the seven treated case-processing offices. The registered test uses those same seven offices, measured over a longer period. That is a real improvement: the model was fixed in advance and the outcome data were new. But it is **not an independent replication**. Anything unusual about those seven offices that produced the original correlation is still present.

There are other problems with the mediation analysis:

- **The sample is effectively 14 offices.** The paper credits the result partly to "a larger sample of office-months". But office-months from the same office are not independent, so the effective sample is still 7 v 7. A confidence interval of 28–66% looks narrow for a mediation estimate based on 14 clusters. The paper should say how clustering was handled.
- **The two mediators are measured with different precision.** Meeting time comes from calendars and is fairly exact. Fatigue is a self-report scale and is noisier. Measurement error biases a mediator's estimated share toward zero, so the 18% for fatigue is likely an **underestimate** relative to the 47% for meetings.
- **The mediators may not be separable.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. How the model divided credit between correlated mediators affects the shares.
- **The registration was not fully blind.** It was filed at month 11, after the investigators had already seen data through month 11, including the 9-month results. That is common and acceptable, but "registered" here does not mean they were blind to the data.

A fair description would be "the meetings association persisted under a pre-specified model in the original offices", rather than "survives a registered test". Varga & Holm's specific worry was that a subgroup correlation would not replicate. This follow-up does not show replication in new offices.

### 2. It is unclear what the system logs measure

The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases". If that means time spent in the case-management system, it excludes meetings. That creates two problems.

**First, the mediation outcome conflicts with the mediator.** If meeting time is not in the denominator, cutting meetings cannot raise output per log-hour by removing unproductive paid time. It could only work indirectly, for example through fewer interruptions and less task-switching. Those are a different mechanism from the one the 9-month report proposed.

**Second, the numbers don't fit a case-work-only measure.** Relative to control:

- Timesheet hours fell about 12%, or roughly 4.5 hours a week.
- Meeting time fell about 3.3 hours.
- So non-meeting time fell only about 1.2 hours, roughly 4%.

If logs measured only case work, which is part of non-meeting time, they should have fallen about 4%. They fell 11%. So either the logs capture something other than case work, or treated staff shifted roughly two hours a week into work that is neither meetings nor logged case work.

The paper also says logs "show slightly more work than timesheets". It bases this on log hours falling 11% versus timesheet hours falling 12%. But that gap could equally come from the meeting reduction rather than from unclaimed work.

The paper needs to say what logs include and exclude. Both the "stricter" 8.5% headline and the mediation result depend on it.

### 3. The control arm was contaminated, probably making the estimate conservative

The "meeting audit" in two control offices at month 15 is presented as an interesting side observation. It is also **contamination of the control arm**. Those offices' output per hour rose about 4%, which narrows the gap between treated and control offices. So the 24-month treatment effect is probably understated somewhat.

The audit may also have been prompted by the trial itself. The 9-month report had publicised the meetings finding, and control staff knew the trial was running. That is a form of spillover the original design aimed to avoid.

The paper should report a sensitivity analysis that excludes those two offices, or at least acknowledge the direction of the bias.

### 4. The decline is not statistically established, and the trend beyond 24 months is unknown

The per-hour gain on timesheets fell from 12.5% (6.9 to 18.4) to 9.8% (4.6 to 15.2). The intervals overlap heavily. The paper's own wording, "consistent with some fading", is appropriate. Section 5 is less careful: "declined by about a quarter" presents the point estimate as an established decline.

With only two time points, the shape of the trend is unknown. The gain might settle around 8–10%, or keep declining. A straight-line extrapolation would not reach zero for several years, but the paper itself rightly criticised Varga & Holm for extrapolating from two points. It should avoid implying the 24-month figure is a stable plateau.

The rebuttal of the "zero by month ten" extrapolation does stand, since the gain is clearly above zero at month 24.

### 5. The Halden follow-up has response bias and a stretched explanation for reversions

- **Only 14 of 23 organisations responded.** Organisations that reverted or did badly are probably less likely to respond, so the reversion count (3 of 14) is likely a minimum.
- **The pattern of reversions is described generously.** The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency, however, cited client deadlines. That is the kind of work the meta-analysis would code as discretionary, and many discretionary organisations have client deadlines. Folding it into the coverage-bound category fits the data to the framework. A better reading is that the binary is leakier than presented: deadline-bound discretionary work can also come under pressure.
- **The reverters' output at reversion was 88–91.** That is a 9–12% fall on records, similar to coverage-bound losses.

### 6. Authors are assessing their own work

The Varden authors are evaluating the hypothesis they proposed. A Halden author, Okafor, is co-authoring a follow-up of Halden's own pilot. Neither affects the arithmetic. But both bear on the framing choices noted above: calling the mediation result "confirmed", and explaining the marketing agency's reversion as a coverage issue. Independent analysis of the 24-month data would help.

### 7. Smaller points

- **The counter arm has no 24-month data.** Its ending at month 12 is the result itself, which is fine. But a follow-up of only the arm that kept going is itself selective. The paper handles this transparently.
- **Quality is still reported as treated v control levels without intervals** (3.2% v 3.0%). This was also the case in the 9-month report.
- **The two-office meeting audit is a before–after comparison in two offices.** The authors' caveats are appropriate. It shows that reorganisation without an hours cut is worth testing as a separate trial arm.

## How the five documents fit together

| Question | Earlier position | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Size of per-hour gain (discretionary) | 23% (Halden) → 8–12% | **~8.5–10% at 24 months**, one randomised trial |
| Output per worker (discretionary) | roughly maintained | **−3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2)**; small loss likely |
| Durability | unknown; meta claimed no decay | **Partial decay**; meta's evidence shown unfit |
| Coverage-bound work | output −9 to −11% | **Abandoned in practice**; +9% cost to restore service |
| Mechanism | unknown | **Meetings ~half, fatigue ~one-fifth** (same offices; fatigue likely understated) |
| "Entirely artifact" | V&H claim | **Not supported** under V&H's own standards |
| Sick leave | −29 to −36% | **Persists (−27%)** |
| Retention | lower resignations | **Persists** (4.1% v 7.9%) |

One open question now matters more than before: **can reorganisation alone, especially cutting meetings, capture much of the gain without reducing hours?** If meetings account for about half the gain, an employer might get that half at no cost in output per worker. The wellbeing and retention effects, though, seem tied to the hours cut. No study has yet tested a "reorganise only" arm. The authors rightly say this trial cannot answer it.

## Fair summary

In one randomised trial of public-sector case processing, a 20% cut in scheduled hours raised output per actual hour by about 8.5–10% after two years, down from about 12.5% at nine months. The decline is suggestive but not statistically established. Output per employee was about 3% below control, with the confidence interval including both no change and a loss of 8%. Quality was unchanged, and the reductions in sick leave and resignations persisted.

Within the same offices, a pre-specified mediation analysis attributes about half the gain to fewer recurring meetings and about a fifth to reduced fatigue, though fatigue is probably understated. This is persistence in the original sample, not an independent replication. It also depends on what the system logs measure, which needs clarification. Contamination of two control offices probably makes the estimate slightly conservative.

In counter work, the scheme was abandoned because waits rose and restoring service would have increased costs.

The evidence now rules out both "entirely artifact" and "no decay". It points to a modest gain in discretionary work, about half of which may be available through reorganisation alone. That possibility remains untested.
